summary: Micah 6 opens as a dispute: Yahweh calls the mountains to hear his case and reminds the people of rescue from Egypt and protection on the way into the land. The chapter then rejects escalating offerings as the answer and states what Yahweh requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God. It closes with charges of dishonest commerce, violence, lies, and the inherited practices of Omri and Ahab, followed by announced loss and ruin.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers Micah’s public accusations into one clear question: what kind of response does God require from a people who claim to belong to him? Its famous verse about justice, mercy, and walking with God is set beside concrete wrongs such as false measures, deceitful weights, violence, and lies.

context.author: The book’s heading attributes the word to Micah of Moresheth; the finished book does not identify everyone involved in arranging the collection.
context.audience: The speeches address Israel and Judah, including Jerusalem, rulers, wealthy people, religious leaders, and the people as a whole.
context.date: Micah’s attributed prophetic activity belongs to the eighth century BCE under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah; the extent of later collection and shaping is disputed.
context.setting: The book centers on Israel and Judah, especially Jerusalem and the Judean countryside, in a world of towns, farms, courts, worship, and imperial pressure.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic dispute and accusation, using summons, questions, remembered rescue, and announced consequences.

outline.heading: The mountains hear Yahweh’s case
outline.note: Yahweh summons the mountains and foundations of the earth as witnesses to his indictment against his people.

outline.heading: Rescue remembered
outline.note: Yahweh asks what burden he has placed on the people, then recalls Egypt, Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Balak, Balaam, Shittim, and Gilgal.

outline.heading: Offerings questioned
outline.note: The speaker asks whether increasingly costly offerings, even a firstborn child, could answer disobedience and sin.

outline.heading: What Yahweh requires
outline.note: The answer is stated as acting justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with God.

outline.heading: The city called to listen
outline.note: Yahweh’s voice addresses the city and names wicked treasures, a short ephah, dishonest scales, deceitful weights, violence, lies, and deceitful speech.

outline.heading: Consequences of the city’s sins
outline.note: The announced judgment touches the body, food, storage, crops, oil, and wine: ordinary labor will not yield secure enjoyment.

outline.heading: Omri and Ahab’s legacy
outline.note: The chapter ends by linking the people’s conduct to the statutes of Omri and works of Ahab’s house, with ruin, hissing, and reproach as the result.

keyVerses.text: For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage. I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
keyVerses.why: This verse names Yahweh’s remembered rescue before the chapter turns to the people’s response.

keyVerses.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s central answer to the questions about offerings in verses 6-7.

keyVerses.text: Shall I tolerate dishonest scales, and a bag of deceitful weights?
keyVerses.why: The verse makes the chapter’s concern with justice concrete in everyday commerce.

keyVerses.text: For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of Ahab’s house. You walk in their counsels, that I may make you a ruin, and your inhabitants a hissing. You will bear the reproach of my people.”
keyVerses.why: The final verse ties the accusations to a destructive pattern of inherited conduct and states the chapter’s closing consequence.

themes: Yahweh’s public case against his people
ruin as consequence for persistent sin

questions.question: Why are the mountains and foundations of the earth addressed?
questions.answer: The chapter pictures Yahweh’s case as a public dispute, with mountains and enduring foundations called to hear the indictment. The scene is poetic and solemn; it does not require reconstructing a complete courtroom procedure.

questions.question: What has Yahweh done for the people, according to this chapter?
questions.answer: Yahweh says he brought the people out of Egypt, redeemed them from bondage, and sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before them. He also asks them to remember Balak’s plan, Balaam’s answer, and the journey from Shittim to Gilgal so they may know his righteous acts.

questions.question: Who are Balak and Balaam, and why are they mentioned?
questions.answer: Balak was Moab’s king, who summoned Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel in Numbers 22. Micah recalls what the king planned and what Balaam answered as part of remembering Yahweh’s righteous acts. The phrase “from Shittim to Gilgal” also recalls Israel’s journey across the Jordan: Joshua 3 begins at Shittim, and Joshua 4 places the camp at Gilgal after the crossing. Micah evokes these events without retelling them.

questions.question: Is verse 7 approving the sacrifice of a firstborn child?
questions.answer: No. Verse 7 belongs to a series of escalating questions about what kind of offering could please Yahweh or address sin. Verse 8 answers by turning away from that escalation toward acting justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with God.

questions.question: What does “walk humbly with your God” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase appears with two other requirements: to act justly and to love mercy. Walking with God describes a continuing way of life, set beside public conduct and followed by accusations about fraud, violence, and lies. The English editions bring out different shades: WEB and KJV say “walk humbly,” Douay-Rheims says “walk solicitous,” and Brenton says “be ready to walk.” Each belongs to the demand for conduct shaped by life with God.

questions.question: What are a “short ephah” and “dishonest scales”?
questions.answer: An undersized measure and dishonest scales cheat people in trade. The chapter treats false measures and deceitful weights as part of the city’s wickedness, not as minor business habits separate from faithfulness to God.

questions.question: What wrongs are charged against the city?
questions.answer: The chapter names treasures of wickedness, a short ephah, dishonest scales, deceitful weights, violence among the rich, lies among the inhabitants, and deceitful speech. These are concrete social and economic accusations.

questions.question: Why do eating, sowing, oil, and wine appear in the judgment?
questions.answer: The announced consequences touch ordinary survival and labor. The people will eat without satisfaction, store without saving, sow without reaping, tread olives without using the oil, and crush grapes without drinking the wine.

questions.question: Who are Omri and Ahab in verse 16?
questions.answer: Omri and his son Ahab were kings of Israel; 1 Kings 16 describes their reigns as evil in Yahweh’s sight. Micah 6:16 invokes Omri’s statutes, the works of Ahab’s house, and their counsels as a pattern the people are still following. The accusation concerns the persistence of those practices and the ruin, hissing, and reproach that follow.

glossary.def: A formal accusation. In this chapter, Yahweh’s indictment is his case against his people.
Rescued or bought out of bondage. Verse 4 uses the word for Yahweh bringing the people out of the house of bondage.
Offerings presented to Yahweh. In verses 6-7, the speaker asks whether such offerings, even in extreme amounts, are what Yahweh wants.
A measure used in trade. A “short ephah” means an unfair measure that cheats the other person.
Scales used deceitfully in commerce. Verse 11 pairs them with “a bag of deceitful weights.”
